Structure-loss paper · urban conflagration

Urban conflagrations as networks · 2026-10-13

Every building as a dot, joined by lines when close enough for fire to jump between them. Three full records: Carlson 2002–22 (353 fires with ≥ 10 destroyed), our 2002–26 record (440), CAL FIRE inspections 2013–25 (110); groups at 30 m and groups of groups at 75 m; network measures, a disease-style spread model on the network, patch sizes and dimensions, a compound-urban-conflagration definition, a 20-measure space of 266 big patches (our record) and a gallery of kinds.

By Carlo Broderick, NCEAS, UC Santa Barbara · 2026-10-13 18:21 PDT

What network thinking adds: towns split into street-sized groups at 30 m that join into larger groups at 50–75 m, and most of the big urban fires are several patches merging rather than one patch: a 'compound' rule picks the same named urban fires as the 30 m rule and is steadier. What it does not add: from the layout of the buildings alone, neither density nor network shape tells us well which buildings in a fire were lost (about 50 on a scale where 50 is a coin flip), and Cat Fong's fitted house-to-house push is far too weak to carry fire through any town on its own: the wildfire (wind, embers, many ignitions) does most of the work. The patch measures boil down to about 5 real dimensions, not 10, and the patches form a continuum rather than distinct types. Tipping distance (where a fire's separate burned groups join into one): usually well above 50 m (median about 125 m in our record); the biggest single jump comes around 70 m; it climbs smoothly, follows the town's own layout, and comes much earlier than random burning would.
Single-linkage hierarchy of destroyed centres; percolation curves; k-core, clustering, bridges, betweenness, Louvain communities, spectral radius of Cat's kernel; independent cascade on the kernel graph; fire-held-out per-fire AUC with fire-cluster bootstrap and Holm. Verdicts (pre-registered): T1 network adds — does not add; T2 spread beyond network — does not add; T3 spread vs density — adds (tiny, ~+1 point); bridges — no sign that bridges matter; merge ratio — has a preferred scale; patch sizes — heavy-tailed but not a power law; compound — compound is a usable definition; merged kind — a continuum from one patch to many; types — no stable types (continuum).

How to read this page

Plain words used on this page. Network: every building is a dot, and a line joins two buildings close enough for fire to jump between them. Link distance: how close (centre to centre) two buildings must be to get a line. Group: buildings joined by a chain of lines. Patch: a group of destroyed buildings. Group of groups: patches found at 30 m that sit in the same group when the link distance is raised (75 m here). Tipping distance: the link distance at which a fire's many separate burned groups suddenly join into one. Urban conflagration: a fire that spreads from building to building through a built-up area, beyond what firefighters can stop. Hover or tap any part of a chart for details; the Plain language / Technical button switches the explanations.

How this relates to Cat Fong's disease model

Cat's model is already a network model: each building is a node, and every pair of buildings is linked with a weight that fades with distance. What the network view adds is the shape of that web (groups, groups of groups, bridges, the distance at which a town becomes one piece) and a threshold question: is the house-to-house push strong enough for fire to keep going by itself? It is not, by a wide margin. What the network view does not add is better prediction of which buildings were lost; for that, where the fire went matters most.

Cat: P_sec = 1 − exp(−β Σ_burned exp(−d/λ)), λ ≈ 12.5 m, β ≈ 0.035, fitted to the residual distance-response after M0 + MTBS adjustment (Carlson Direct 2013–22). Here: the same kernel as a weighted graph; spectral radius per 30 m component (SIR-percolation bound), independent-cascade simulations as predictors, and single-linkage hierarchy for the multi-scale structure. The network view complements rather than replaces the kernel fit.

1 · The idea in pictures

The 30 m rule we used before finds street-sized groups. Raising the link distance shows how those groups join: groups of groups.

Houses as dots, joined by lines (illustration)

An illustration, not a real town: 29 houses, 7 trees. Filled houses were destroyed; houses with a white dot survived. Drag the slider: at 30 m the houses on each street join into street groups; at 50–75 m nearby street groups join into groups of groups; past ~160 m the whole town is one group. This is the structure the owner described as 'groups linked to groups'.Single linkage on centres: groups at distance d are the connected components of the graph with edges ≤ d, equivalently the minimum spanning tree cut at d. Tipping distance across all fires: where do the burned groups join?

Plain words: tipping distance is the link distance at which a fire's many separate burned groups are about to join into one (the second-biggest group is largest just before it is swallowed). Across fires with at least 100 destroyed it is usually well above 50 m (median 125, 125 and 135 m); only 9 of 109 fires in our record tip at 40–60 m. The biggest single jump of the biggest group comes earlier, around 65–70 m: that is the change the owner saw between the 50 m and 75 m maps; the number of separate burned groups of 50 or more peaks a little later (median about 85 m in our record, in the 35 fires that have two or more). Almost every fire climbs smoothly rather than jumping. The burned buildings tip at about the same distance as the town itself (so the tipping point is mostly the town's layout), but much earlier than random burning would (the losses are clumped).Pre-registered (amendment 2) verdicts: T8 smooth climbs; T9 vs town: the tipping point is town layout; T9 vs random: no different from random burning (only fires where random burning tips inside 150 m enter; most do not, so this verdict is censored-limited; the censoring-aware sign test, exploratory, says destroyed tips earlier in 81 of 87 fires in our record); T10: not near 50 m.

3 · Does the network explain which buildings were lost?

Network theory's first promise: maybe who is connected to whom explains losses better than how many neighbours a building has.

Gain from network shape and from spread on the network, over plain density

Inside a fire, the layout of the buildings tells us little about which ones were lost: density and position alone score about 51, 50 and 52 (50 = coin flip). Adding network shape (group sizes, k-core, clustering, bridges, spreading strength) or a disease-style spread on the network adds at most about 1–2 points. What decides which buildings burn is mostly where the fire went (wind, embers, the fire front), which the building layout does not hold.Pre-registered T1–T3 (Holm over 9): {'T1 network adds to density': 'does not add', 'T2 spread adds beyond network': 'does not add', 'T3 spread alone vs density': 'adds'}. Model: L2 logistic, 10 fire-grouped folds; spread features = independent cascade on the kernel graph (β chosen inside training folds from 0.035–1; seeds uniform or edge-weighted). Robustness rows: features as within-fire z-scores. Exploratory: AUC inside 500 m neighbourhoods (p32_pred_auc.csv).

4 · Cat Fong's disease model, seen as a network

Cat used a disease (contagion) model. A network is the natural home for that model: same kernel, but now we can ask whether the network lets the 'disease' spread on its own.

How strong would the house-to-house push have to be for fire to keep itself going?

Cat's model says each burning building nearby slightly raises a building's chance of burning (fitted push β ≈ 0.035, fading over ~12.5 m). On the real networks, that push is far too weak for fire to keep going from house to house on its own: the push would have to be about 34 times stronger in the median fire, and 9 times in Tubbs 2017, 13 times in Camp 2018, 21 times in Marshall 2021, 12 times in Eaton 2025, 21 times in Lahaina 2023 even in the big urban fires. So urban conflagrations need the wildfire's help (embers, wind, many ignitions at once) to get going; the house-to-house effect amplifies rather than drives them.Network spreading threshold: for a contagion with transmission matrix P (p_ij = 1 − exp(−β K_ij), K = exp(−d/12.5 m), pairs ≤ 60 m), ρ(P) < 1 rules out a self-sustaining outbreak (Wang et al. 2003; Chakrabarti et al. 2008). Max ρ(P) at β = 0.035 over all fires: 0.20 / 0.20 / 0.14. β_crit = 1/ρ(K) per fire's largest 30 m group.

5 · Do 'bridges' between groups carry fire?

Neighbouring groups: is the second group lost more often when the bridge is short?

Where one group of buildings was lost, its neighbouring group was also lost about two times in three. Whether the closest pair of buildings between them (the 'bridge') was short or long made no clear difference once the distance between the groups' centres is known. Verdict (pre-set): no sign that bridges matter.Pairs of 30 m standing groups (≥ 5 buildings each, closest gap ≤ 150 m, at least one ≥ 50% destroyed); outcome both lost; fire fixed-effects logistic; 1,000-draw fire bootstrap; Holm over 3 records on the gap term.

6 · Groups of groups: is it a fractal?

The owner asked whether the patches-joining-patches structure is 'kind of like a fractal'.

Doubling the link distance: how many groups merge?

A true fractal would merge groups at the same rate at every scale. It does not: each doubling from 30 to 480 m merges more groups than the one before (slope above zero in all three records). There are preferred scales: street groups below ~30 m, neighbourhoods at 50–300 m, then whole towns. Verdict (pre-set): has a preferred scale.Merge ratio N(d)/N(2d) of single-linkage components, fires ≥ 100 destroyed; per-fire slope of log ratio on log d; bar for 'self-similar': 95% interval inside ±0.10.

Patch sizes: a few huge, very many small

Most patches are one or two buildings; a few hold hundreds. The size spread is heavy-tailed, but a strict power law (the usual fractal signature) is not clearly better than a lognormal: verdict heavy-tailed but not a power law.Discrete power law (x_min by KS) vs lognormal / exponential / power law with cut-off, Vuong tests, Holm over records; pooled 30 m patches. Fractal dimension: are the losses more clumped than the town?

Pair counting says yes: destroyed buildings sit closer together than an equal number of buildings picked at random from the same town (lower number). Box counting moves the other way, because it mostly measures that the losses fill only part of the fire area. So 'more clumped at short range' holds; a single fractal dimension does not describe the pattern.Box-counting (50–800 m, 4 offsets) and correlation dimension (25–800 m) of destroyed-inside vs 20 random-labelling draws; fires ≥ 100 destroyed; Holm over 6. Verdicts: box can't tell; pair counting destroyed pattern more clumped than the town.

7 · A compound urban conflagration

If patches close together are 'multiple urban conflagrations coming together', that can be written down as a rule and tested.

Compound (several patches close together) vs a single big patch

Proposed definition: a compound urban conflagration is a 75 m group of destroyed buildings that holds at least two patches of 20 or more (patches found with 30 m links). It picks 8, 10 and 5 fires, catches exactly the same named urban fires as the 30 m rule with no spread-out fire, and is steadier when its settings move (stability 0.89, 0.91, 0.94). In our record it differs from the 30 m rule only at the edges (Sandalwood and Woolsey: one big patch, not several; Dixie and Erskine: several patches, none of 50). Compound groups hold 26%, 31% and 43% of all destroyed buildings in the three records.Scored as PA34 against the frozen reference list; stability = mean Jaccard over 5 neighbouring settings; bar (pre-set): stability ≥ 0.6 in all records, balanced accuracy ≥ the 30 m rule in 2 of 3, no more W fires. Verdict: compound is a usable definition. Share of the largest 30 m patch inside 75 m groups ≥ 50: Silverman test, verdict 'a continuum from one patch to many'.

8 · The many-dimension space

The owner asked for a 10-dimensional space. We assembled one table of 20 measures per big patch and asked how many dimensions it really has.

How many real dimensions?

We measured 20 things about each big patch (≥ 20 destroyed): spacing, network, groups of groups, trees, slope, depth into town, building kinds and more. They boil down to 5, 5 and 5 real dimensions in the three records (72% of the variation in our record), not 10.PCA on standardised measures; dimensions kept by Horn's parallel analysis (eigenvalue above the 95th percentile of 200 column-permuted copies).

Patches in the first two dimensions, by type

Each dot is a patch. The mixture model splits them into 3 groups in our record, but the split is not stable when fires are resampled (agreement 0.37 on a 0–1 scale; needed 0.6). Verdict: no stable types (continuum). The groups mostly separate big fires from each other rather than kinds of burning, and tree-helped chains (squares) are spread across them. Wind was kept out of the space; described afterwards, the type made of patches from a handful of the largest fires burned in much stronger gusts (hover a dot for its fire's peak gust).Gaussian mixtures k = 1–8 on the kept components (BIC); 200 fire-bootstrap refits, adjusted Rand index vs full-data labels: R1 0.67, R2 0.37, R3 0.56.

9 · Kinds of urban conflagration

A gallery of kinds, with how each can be measured

Beyond house-to-house, tree-to-house and wind-driven, the data and the literature point to other kinds. Each card says what it looks like, how we measured it, how many big patches or fires show it in each record, and which public data could test it. Kinds overlap: one fire can hold several.Patch-level signatures on 30 m patches ≥ 20 destroyed; fire-level signatures on fires ≥ 50 destroyed; wind and timing described only (CLAUDE.md: fire weather never enters a definition built from what burned).

House-to-house

Buildings so close that a burning house ignites the next one, street after street.

Carlson 2002–22: 121 of 125 patches
Our 2002–26 record: 259 of 266 patches
CAL FIRE inspections 2013–25: 163 of 195 patches
Examples: Almeda Drive 2020, Tubbs 2017, Palisades 2025, Sayre 2008
Almost every big patch meets this signature (97% in our record): on its own it does not separate kinds.

Status: Measured (patch: completeness ≥ 80% and spacing ≤ 25 m).

Data: Public data: building footprints and loss records.

House-and-tree

Fire chains from house to house through trees and yards between them.

Carlson 2002–22: 54 of 125 patches
Our 2002–26 record: 142 of 266 patches
CAL FIRE inspections 2013–25: 84 of 195 patches
Examples: Eaton 2025, Palisades 2025, Camp 2018, Glass 2020

Status: Measured by the patch study (PA40 tree links through ≥ 25% canopy).

Data: Public data: USFS tree canopy cover before the fire.

Wind-driven

Strong winds push flames and embers across gaps that would normally stop the fire.

Status: Described only, never part of a definition (wind is a property of the fire, not of what burned). Gridded wind at the town is being built (PA41).

Data: Public data: HRRR, RTMA, ERA5, RAWS weather.

Compound (patches merging)

Several separate patches of 20 or more lost buildings close together, joining at 75 m into one larger burn.

Carlson 2002–22: 8 of 140 fires
Our 2002–26 record: 10 of 162 fires
CAL FIRE inspections 2013–25: 5 of 51 fires
Examples: Camp 2018, Eaton 2025, Palisades 2025, Tubbs 2017

Status: Measured here; a usable definition by the pre-set bar.

Data: Public data: loss records only.

Ember storm / spotting

Embers carried far ahead land on scattered houses: losses sit alone, far from other losses.

Carlson 2002–22: 9 of 140 fires
Our 2002–26 record: 11 of 162 fires
CAL FIRE inspections 2013–25: 13 of 51 fires
Examples: Cameron Peak 2020, Spring Creek 2018, Limebelt 2015, Hayman 2002

Status: Measured (fire level: at least half of losses with no other loss within 100 m).

Data: Public data: loss records; wind direction for checks.

Several separate patches

Many patches at once can overwhelm firefighting; whether they burned at the same time needs timing.

Carlson 2002–22: 7 of 140 fires
Our 2002–26 record: 9 of 162 fires
CAL FIRE inspections 2013–25: 5 of 51 fires
Examples: Camp 2018, Eaton 2025, Palisades 2025, Tubbs 2017

Status: Counted here (3+ patches of ≥ 20); 'at the same time' needs satellite timing (PA41).

Data: Public data: FIRMS / GOES fire detections.

Mobile-home park burn

Closely packed manufactured homes burn as one block.

Carlson 2002–22: 44 of 125 patches
Our 2002–26 record: 44 of 266 patches
CAL FIRE inspections 2013–25: 38 of 195 patches
Examples: Almeda Drive 2020, Tubbs 2017, Sayre 2008, Woolsey 2018

Status: Measured (patch: mobile-home share ≥ 50%; Carlson and CAL FIRE building types).

Data: Public data: CAL FIRE inspections, HIFLD mobile-home parks (15 states).

Commercial or dense multi-unit core

Apartments, shops and offices in a town centre burn together (e.g. Lahaina Front Street).

Carlson 2002–22: 4 of 125 patches
Our 2002–26 record: 4 of 266 patches
CAL FIRE inspections 2013–25: 57 of 195 patches
Examples: Glass 2020, Lilac 5 2017, Tubbs 2017

Status: Measured where building types exist (CAL FIRE inspections mostly).

Data: Public data: CAL FIRE inspection types; elsewhere no national building-type layer.

Deep penetration

Fire carried by buildings far into town, not just at the wildland edge.

Carlson 2002–22: 50 of 125 patches
Our 2002–26 record: 183 of 266 patches
CAL FIRE inspections 2013–25: 143 of 195 patches
Examples: Tubbs 2017, Eaton 2025, Palisades 2025, Camp 2018

Status: Measured (patch: median depth into the built-up area ≥ 300 m).

Data: Public data: building footprints.

Edge-only losses

Losses only along the wildland edge; the town interior survives.

Carlson 2002–22: 25 of 125 patches
Our 2002–26 record: 26 of 266 patches
CAL FIRE inspections 2013–25: 22 of 195 patches
Examples: Glass 2020, Almeda Drive 2020, Hennessey 2020, Rice 2007

Status: Measured (patch: median depth ≤ 100 m).

Data: Public data: building footprints.

Long, narrow run

A patch stretched along one direction, as when wind or a slope drives the fire.

Carlson 2002–22: 34 of 125 patches
Our 2002–26 record: 90 of 266 patches
CAL FIRE inspections 2013–25: 78 of 195 patches
Examples: Almeda Drive 2020, Tubbs 2017, Palisades 2025, Camp 2018

Status: Shape measured (long/short axis ≥ 3); whether wind or slope drove it needs wind direction (PA41).

Data: Public data: 3DEP slope, gridded wind direction.

Steep-slope or downslope-wind run

Fire running up a steep slope, or pushed downhill by downslope winds (e.g. Diablo, Santa Ana).

Carlson 2002–22: 0 of 125 patches
Our 2002–26 record: 1 of 266 patches
CAL FIRE inspections 2013–25: 1 of 195 patches
Examples: Palisades 2025

Status: Slope measured (median ≥ 15°: very rare among big patches); downslope wind direction not built yet.

Data: Public data: 3DEP elevation; gridded wind.

Night-time run

The town burns at night, when people are asleep and firefighting is harder.

Carlson 2002–22: 67 of 140 fires
Our 2002–26 record: 74 of 162 fires
CAL FIRE inspections 2013–25: 2 of 51 fires
Examples: Eaton 2025, Tubbs 2017, Carr 2018, Bastrop County Complex 2011

Status: Described only (start of the town burn from FIRMS satellite timing, PA41).

Data: Public data: FIRMS / GOES detection times.

How this panel was checked
  • Every count is read from p32_kinds_gallery.csv; denominators (patches or fires) are printed on each card.
  • Signatures are simple stated thresholds, not fitted; they describe, they do not define.
  • CAL FIRE inspection fires have no satellite timing joined yet (night-time count shows 0 for that record).
